claim: African trypanosomes cause sleeping sickness in humans and nagana in cattle.
source: African trypanosomes cause sleeping sickness in humans and nagana in cattle.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in parasitology, supported by scientific consensus and historical knowledge.

claim: African trypanosomes are transmitted by the bloodsucking tsetse fly.
source: These unicellular parasites are transmitted by the bloodsucking tsetse fly.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about trypanosome transmission.

claim: In the mammalian host's circulation, proliferating slender stage cells differentiate into cell cycle-arrested stumpy stage cells when they reach high population densities.
source: In the mammalian host's circulation, proliferating slender stage cells differentiate into cell cycle-arrested stumpy stage cells when they reach high population densities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome life cycle stages, supported by previous research.

claim: The slender-to-stumpy stage transition auto-regulates the parasite load in the host.
source: This stage transition is thought to fulfil two main functions: first, it auto-regulates the parasite load in the host
evidence: This is a previously held view in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: The stumpy stage is regarded as the only stage capable of successful vector transmission.
source: second, the stumpy stage is regarded as the only stage capable of successful vector transmission.
evidence: This represents the traditional view in the field that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Proliferating slender stage trypanosomes express the mRNA and protein of a known stumpy stage marker.
source: Here, we show that proliferating slender stage trypanosomes express the mRNA and protein of a known stumpy stage marker
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slender stage trypanosomes complete the complex life cycle in the fly as successfully as the stumpy stage.
source: complete the complex life cycle in the fly as successfully as the stumpy stage
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data on tsetse fly infections.

claim: Only a single trypanosome parasite is required for productive infection of the tsetse fly.
source: require only a single parasite for productive infection
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing infections with very low parasite numbers.

claim: The findings suggest a reassessment of the traditional view of the trypanosome life cycle.
source: These findings suggest a reassessment of the traditional view of the trypanosome life cycle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The findings may provide a solution to the paradox of successful transmission of parasites in chronic infections despite low parasitemia.
source: They may also provide a solution to a long-lasting paradox, namely the successful transmission of parasites in chronic infections, despite low parasitemia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the implications of the findings.

claim: Trypanosomes are among the most successful parasites.
source: Trypanosomes are among the most successful parasites.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge about trypanosome biology and distribution.

claim: Trypanosomes infect all vertebrate classes, from fish to mammals.
source: These flagellated protists infect all vertebrate classes, from fish to mammals, and can cause devastating diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the host range of trypanosomes.

claim: Trypanosoma brucei brucei has emerged as a genetic and cell biological model parasite.
source: The most intensively s tudied African trypanosome subspecies is Trypanosoma brucei brucei, which in the past decades has emerged as a genetic and cell biological model parasite.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the use of T. brucei in research.

claim: The life cycle of T. brucei was initially elucidated more than a century ago.
source: The life cycle of T. brucei was initially elucidated more than a century ago.
evidence: This is historical knowledge about trypanosome research.

claim: Trypanosomes undergo a full developmental program in the tsetse fly to become infective to the mammalian host.
source: As part of their life cycle, the trypanosomes undergo a full developmental program in the tsetse fly in order to become infective to the mammalian host (Koch, 1909).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by historical citations.

claim: Kleine in 1909 showed that trypanosome transmission was not a purely mechanical event.
source: This finding, made by Kleine in 1909, showed that transmission was not a purely mechanical event (Kleine, 1909).
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by citation.

claim: The life cycle in the fly can take up to several weeks to complete.
source: Kleine subsequently found that the life cycle in the fly could take up to several weeks to complete, a discovery that was shortly afterwards confirmed by Bruce et al., 1909.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by historical citations.

claim: After entering the tsetse midgut, trypanosomes differentiate into the proliferative procyclic stage.
source: Upon entering the tsetse midgut, the trypanosomes differentiate into the proliferative procyclic stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome development in the tsetse fly.

claim: Parasites must pass the peritrophic matrix to continue their development in the tsetse fly.
source: Once established in the midgut, the parasites must pass the peritrophic matrix, a protective sleeve that separates the bloodmeal from midgut tissue.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome migration in the tsetse fly.

claim: Parasites swim up the endotrophic space to the proventriculus to cross the peritrophic matrix.
source: To do this, the parasites are thought to swim up the endotrophic space to the proventriculus, the site of peritrophic matrix synthesis, where they are able to cross to the ectotrophic space (Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Procyclic trypanosomes may become the cell-cycle arrested mesocyclic stage in the ectotrophic anterior midgut.
source: After having crossed the peritrophic matrix and entered the ectroperitrophic space, procyclic trypanosomes may either further colonise the ectotrophic anterior midgut, becoming the cell-cycle arrested mesocyclic stage, or continue directly to the proventriculus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome development stages.

claim: In the proventriculus, trypanosomes develop into the long, proliferative epimastigote stage.
source: In the proventriculus, trypanosomes further develop into the long, proliferative epimastigote stage (Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Epimastigotes undergo asymmetric division to generate a long and a short daughter cell while swimming to the salivary glands.
source: The epimastigotes then swim from the proventriculus to the salivary glands, while undergoing an asymmetric division to generate a long and a short daughter cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epimastigote development.

claim: The long daughter cell from epimastigote division is thought to die while the short one attaches to the salivary gland epithelium.
source: Once in the salivary gland, the long daughter cell is thought to die while the small one attaches via its flagellum to the salivary gland epithelium (Vickerman, 1969).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Attached epimastigotes produce either more attached epimastigote daughter cells or freely swimming, cell cycle-arrested metacyclic trypanosomes.
source: The attached epimastigotes are proliferative, producing either more attached epimastigote daughter cells or freely swimming, cell cycle-arrested metacyclic trypanosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epimastigote development in salivary glands.

claim: The metacyclic stage is the only mammalian-infective stage.
source: As early as 1911, it was clear that the metacyclic stage (at that time called metatrypanosomes) is the only mammalian-infective stage (Bruce et al., 1911).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by historical citation.

claim: Trypanosomes have been found in many different organs in the mammalian host, including brain, skin, and fat.
source: In the mammalian host, trypanosomes have been found in many different organs, including brain, skin, and fat, but are hard to study experimentally (Capewell et al., 2016; Goodwin, 1970; Krüger et al., 2018; Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The two main stages found in the bloodstream are the proliferating slender bloodstream stage and the cell cycle-arrested stumpy bloodstream stage.
source: The two main stages found in the bloodstream, and the best-characterised experimentally, are the proliferating slender bloodstream stage and the cell cycle-arrested stumpy bloodstream stage (Krüger et al., 2018; Matthews et al., 2004; Vickerman, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The stumpy stage is formed in response to quorum sensing of the stumpy induction factor (SIF).
source: The stumpy stage is formed in response to quorum sensing of the stumpy induction factor (SIF), a signal produced by slender bloodstream trypanosomes (Vassella et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The stumpy stage only survives for 2–3 days after formation.
source: As the stumpy stage only survives for 2–3 days after formation, the generation of stumpy parasites is thought to control the burden the parasites impose on the host (Turner et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PAD1 is the first recognised molecular marker for stumpy stage trypanosomes.
source: The SIF pathway that controls the slender-to-stumpy transition has been described down to the molecular level, with the protein associated with differentiation (PAD1) being the first recognised molecular marker for the stumpy stage trypanosomes (Dean et al., 2009; Mony and Matthews, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The stumpy pathway can be triggered independently of SIF.
source: More recently, it was also shown that the stumpy pathway can be triggered independently of SIF, although the extent to which this occurs in the general population remains unclear (Batram et al., 2014; Zimmermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The stumpy stage is believed to be the only life cycle stage that can infect the tsetse fly.
source: Besides its proposed role in controlling parasitaemia in the mammalian host, the stumpy stage has a second essential function in the trypanosome life cycle: it is believed to be the only life cycle stage that can infect the tsetse fly (Rico et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the traditional view in the field, supported by citation, which the manuscript challenges.

claim: Arrest of the cell cycle and differentiation to the stumpy stage are presumed essential for developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage.
source: Thus, arrest of the cell cycle and differentiation to the stumpy stage are presumed essential for developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage.
evidence: This is the traditional view in the field that the manuscript challenges.

claim: Robertson suggested in 1912 that the short, stumpy bloodstream trypanosomes represent the fly-infective stage.
source: As early as 1912, Robertson suggested that the short, stumpy bloodstream trypanosomes represent the fly-infective stage (Robertson, 1912).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The discovery of quorum sensing and SIF in the 1990s made the stumpy-only transmission assumption generally accepted.
source: While this assumption was questioned several times throughout the 20th century, the discovery of quorum sensing and SIF in the 1990s made it become generally accepted (Vassella et al., 1997).
evidence: This is historical knowledge about the field, supported by citation.

claim: Chronic trypanosome infections are characterised by low blood parasitemia.
source: Although trypanosomes might be found at higher densities in the skin (Capewell et al., 2016), chronic trypanosome infections are characterised by low blood parasitemia, meaning that the chance of a tsetse fly ingesting any trypanosomes, let alone short-lived stumpy ones, is also very low (Frezil, 1971; Wombou Toukam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mathematical models have been developed to explain how limited numbers of short-lived stumpy cells can guarantee tsetse fly infection.
source: Mathematical models have been developed that aim to explain how the limited number of short-lived stumpy cells in the host blood and interstitial fluids can guarantee the infection of the tsetse fly, which is essential for the survival of the species (Capewell et al., 2019; MacGregor and Matthews, 2008; Seed and Black, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Very few trypanosomes are necessary to infect a tsetse fly.
source: First, systematic quantification of infection efficiencies showed that very few trypanosomes are necessary to infect a tsetse fly, and in fact just one is sufficient.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Slender stages proved at least as competent at infecting flies as stumpy stages.
source: Second, and wholly unexpectedly, slender stages proved at least as competent at infecting flies as stumpy stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The findings suggest greater plasticity in the life cycle than supposed.
source: These findings suggest greater plasticity in the life cycle than supposed, prompting a reassessment of the current rigid view of the process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Slender and stumpy bloodstream stage trypanosomes can be distinguished based on cell cycle, morphological, and metabolic criteria.
source: Slender and stumpy bloodstream stage trypanosomes can be distinguished based on cell cycle, morphological, and metabolic criteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claim: The prescribed sequence of kinetoplast and nucleus replication (1K1N, 2K1N, 2K2N) allows cell cycle stage to be inferred.
source: The genome of the single mitochondrion (kinetoplast, K) and the cell nucleus (N) can be readily visualised using DNA stains, and their prescribed sequence of replication (1K1N, 2K1N, 2K2N) allows cell cycle stage to be inferred (Sherwin and Gull, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Slender cells are found in all three K/N ratios, while stumpy cells are found only as 1K1N cells.
source: Slender cells are found in all three K/N ratios, while stumpy cells, which are cell cycle-arrested, are found only as 1K1N cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of PAD1 is accepted as a marker for development to the stumpy stage.
source: Expression of the protein associated with differentiation 1 (PAD1) is accepted as a marker for development to the stumpy stage (Dean et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The 3'UTR of the PAD1 gene regulates the expression of pad1.
source: As the 3'UTR of the PAD1 gene regulates the expression of pad1 (MacGregor and Matthews, 2012), cells expressing an NLS-GFP reporter fused to the 3' UTR of the PAD1 gene (GFP:PAD1UTR) will have GFP-positive nuclei when the PAD1 gene is active.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Slender cells are GFP-negative; stumpy cells are GFP-positive when using the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter.
source: Hence, slender cells are GFP-negative; stumpy cells are GFP-positive (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: The validity of the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter as an indicator for the activation of the PAD1 pathway has been reported previously.
source: The validity of the GFP:PAD1UTR reporter as an indicator for the activation of the PAD1 pathway has been reported previously (Batram et al., 2014; Zimmermann et al., 2017), and was further corroborated by co-staining with an antibody against the PAD1 protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and additional data in the manuscript.

claim: Stumpy cells can be formed independently of high cell population density by ectopic expression of a second VSG isoform.
source: We have previously shown that stumpy cells can be formed independently of high cell population density by ectopic expression of a second variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) isoform, a process that mimics one of the pathways involved in trypanosome antigenic variation (Batram et al., 2014; Cross, 1975; Hertz-Fowler et al., 2008; Zimmermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: ES-attenuated stumpy cells can complete the developmental cycle in the tsetse fly.
source: These so-called expression site (ES)-attenuated stumpy cells can complete the developmental cycle in the tsetse fly (Zimmermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation.

claim: A feeding tsetse typically ingests about 20 µl of blood.
source: A feeding tsetse typically ingests about 20 µl of blood (Gibson and Bailey, 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The uptake of just two stumpy parasites on average produced robust infections of tsetse midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands.
source: Remarkably, the uptake, on average, of just two stumpy parasites of either cell line produced robust infections of tsetse midgut (MG), proventriculus (PV), and salivary glands (SG) (Figure 1D; Figure 2A, columns 5–7, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Ingestion of even a single stumpy cell on average was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of all tsetse.
source: Ingestion, on average, of even a single stumpy cell was sufficient to produce salivary gland infections in almost 5% of all tsetse (Figure 2A, row v).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: When the stumpy parasite number was reduced to 0.2 cells on average per bloodmeal, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections.
source: When the stumpy parasite number was further reduced to 0.2 cells on average per bloodmeal, meaning only every 5th fly would receive a stumpy cell, 0.9% of flies still acquired salivary gland infections (Figure 2A, row vi).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: The transmission index (TI) is defined as the ratio of salivary gland to midgut infections.
source: The TI has been previously defined as the ratio of salivary gland to midgut infections and hence, it is a measure for successful passage through the second part of the trypanosome tsetse cycle, where trypanosomes are again infective to a mammalian host (Figures 1B, 3-5)(Peacock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citation.

claim: For flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (TI = 0.29) and ES-induced (TI = 0.31) stumpy trypanosomes.
source: We found that for flies infected with two trypanosomes on average, the TI was comparable between SIF-induced (TI = 0.29) and ES-induced (TI = 0.31) stumpy trypanosomes (Figure 2A, rows iii-iv; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: A TI of 0.23 was observed in flies ingesting on average one trypanosome.
source: A similar TI of 0.23 was observed in flies ingesting on average one trypanosome (Figure 2A, row v; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: SIF- and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the weeks-long, multi-step fly cycle.
source: Thus, our data not only clearly show that SIF- and ES-induced stumpy parasites are equally efficient in completing the weeks-long, multi-step fly cycle
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on transmission indices.

claim: T. brucei infects the salivary glands, while T. congolense infects the proboscis.
source: While this may seem comparable with an observation that has been made before for Trypanosoma congolense (Maudlin and Welburn, 1989), the migration through the fly differs between the two species: T. brucei infects the salivary glands, while T. congolense infects the proboscis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences between trypanosome species, supported by citation.

claim: The tsetse fly is much more susceptible to infections with T. congolense than with T. brucei.
source: The tsetse fly, however, is much more susceptible to infections with T. congolense than with T. brucei, with a nearly 5-fold increase in percent T. congolense proboscis infections as compared to T. brucei salivary gland infections.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in infection susceptibility between trypanosome species.

claim: Very low numbers of T. brucei stumpy cells can successfully establish mature tsetse fly infections.
source: Our results demonstrate that very low numbers of T. brucei stumpy cells can also successfully establish mature tsetse fly infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Slender parasites were not only viable in the midgut, but also infected the proventriculus and the salivary glands.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that slender parasites were not only viable in the midgut, but also infected the proventriculus and the salivary glands. (Figure 2A, rows vii-xi; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: One slender parasite on average was sufficient to establish midgut infections.
source: Even one slender parasite was on average sufficient to establish midgut infections, proving that slender and stumpy parasites are, in principle, equally viable in the tsetse midgut.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The infection efficiency was similar when flies were fed with either 20 stumpy trypanosomes or 20 pleomorphic slender trypanosomes.
source: The infection efficiency, measured using TI, was similar when the flies were fed with either 20 stumpy trypanosomes or 20 pleomorphic slender trypanosomes (Figure 2A, compare TI in column eight for rows ii and vii).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites each, the TI was higher for slender cells (0.60) than for stumpy cells (0.31).
source: When flies were fed with an average of two slender parasites each, the TI was actually higher for slender cells (0.60) than for stumpy cells (0.31) (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: When given, on average, just one PAD1-negative slender cell per bloodmeal, parasite infections were established in the midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands with incidences of 4.7%, 4.1%, and 2.0% respectively, at a TI of 0.44.
source: Next, when given, on average, just one PAD1-negative slender cell per bloodmeal, parasite infections were still established in the midgut, proventriculus, and salivary glands with incidences of 4.7%, 4.1%, and 2.0% respectively, at a TI of 0.44 (Figure 2A, row x; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3.

claim: Infections with, on average, two freshly-differentiated slender trypanosomes per bloodmeal revealed 6.3% midgut and 2.7% salivary gland infections with a transmission index of 0.43.
source: Infections with, on average, two freshly-differentiated slender trypanosomes per bloodmeal revealed 6.3% midgut and 2.7% salivary gland infections. The transmission index was 0.43 (Figure 2A. row xiii).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2A.

claim: Monomorphic trypanosomes are able to infect the tsetse midgut, but they are incapable of establishing robust infections and completing the developmental cycle in the fly.
source: Monomorphic trypanosomes are able to infect the tsetse midgut, but they are incapable of establishing robust infections and completing the developmental cycle in the fly (Herder et al., 2007; Peacock et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: No salivary gland infections were seen using monomorphic cells, even at high infection numbers.
source: As expected, no salivary gland infections were seen using these cells, even at high infection numbers.
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment, consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish a fly midgut infection.
source: Interestingly, we found that even two monomorphic slender parasites could establish a fly midgut infection (Figure 2A, row xv).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment, supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Infection of the tsetse midgut is independent of the capacity for developmental progression and the infective dose, and it does not require the stumpy life cycle stage.
source: Thus, infection of the tsetse midgut is independent of the capacity for developmental progression and the infective dose, and it does not require the stumpy life cycle stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on monomorphic and slender infections.

claim: The finding challenges the assumption that slender parasites are selectively eliminated from the parasite population and that only stumpy trypanosomes can survive the harsh conditions in the tsetse crop and midgut.
source: This finding also challenges the assumption that slender parasites are selectively eliminated from the parasite population and that only stumpy trypanosomes can survive the harsh conditions thought to prevail within the tsetse crop and midgut (Nolan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings, challenging previous assumptions supported by citation.

claim: The ES-attenuated cells showed similar midgut, proventriculus, and salivary gland infection incidence as either the stumpy or slender stage.
source: The ES-attenuated cells showed similar midgut, proventriculus, and salivary gland infection incidence as either the stumpy or slender stage (Figure 2A, rows ii-iii and vii-viii, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The SIF-induced stumpy cells appeared more effective in establishing midgut infections than their slender counterparts.
source: The SIF-induced stumpy cells, however, appeared more effective in establishing midgut infections than their slender counterparts (Figure 2A, rows iv-vi and ix-xi, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than those with the same numbers of stumpy cells.
source: First, the infections with one to two slender cells produced higher TI values than those with the same numbers of stumpy cells (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The proliferative slender cells are more capable of progressing from a midgut infection to a salivary gland one, and thus have at least comparable overall developmental competence to the stumpy stage.
source: This suggests that the proliferative slender cells are actually more capable of progressing from a midgut infection to a salivary gland one, and thus have at least comparable overall developmental competence to the stumpy stage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the transmission index data.

claim: The lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the TI as a relative measure.
source: Second, the lack of correlation between infective dose and midgut infections underlines the importance of the TI as a relative measure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
source: What is biologically relevant is not the initiation of infection but the completion of the tsetse passage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: A single T. brucei cell (either slender or stumpy) can infect the tsetse fly.
source: In summary, our experiments not only establish that a single T. brucei cell (either slender or stumpy) can infect the tsetse fly
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claim: Infections established by slender cells can result in efficient completion of the passage through the tsetse fly.
source: but also indicate that infections established by slender cells can still result in efficient completion of the passage through the tsetse fly.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claim: Ingested stumpy cells reactivate the cell cycle, begin to express the EP procyclin protein on their cell surface, and differentiate to the procyclic life cycle stage.
source: The canonical version of events is that ingested stumpy (i.e. PAD1-positive) cells reactivate the cell cycle, begin to express the EP procyclin protein on their cell surface, and differentiate to the procyclic life cycle stage (Dean et al., 2009; Matthews and Gull, 1994; Mowatt and Clayton, 1987; Richardson et al., 1988; Roditi et al., 1989; Ziegelbauer and Overath, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the canonical differentiation pathway, supported by multiple citations.

claim: As early as 2 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, 0.8% of 2K1N dividing trypanosomes with a nuclear PAD1 signal could be observed.
source: As early as 2 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, a few (0.8%) 2K1N dividing trypanosomes with a nuclear PAD1 signal could be observed (Figure 5A, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: After 8 hr, half (50.4%) of all trypanosomes in the explants were PAD1-positive.
source: After 8 hr however, half (38.3+6.8+5.3=50.4%) of all trypanosomes in the explants were PAD1-positive (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1 shows summed cell cycle category values for PAD1-positive cells).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5A and supplement.

claim: After 24 hr, 84.3% of the parasites expressed PAD1, and 9.8% had already initiated developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage.
source: After 24 hr, 84.3% (56.3+15.0+13.0) of the parasites expressed PAD1. Of these, 9.8% had already initiated developmental progression to the procyclic insect stage, as evidenced by EP1:YFP fluorescence on their cell surface (Figure 6, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: At 48 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, virtually the entire trypanosome population (91.8%) expressed PAD1, and almost one fifth (19.1%) of cells were EP1-positive.
source: At 48 hr post-infection with slender trypanosomes, virtually the entire trypanosome population (91.8%) expressed PAD1, and almost one fifth (19.1%) of cells were EP1-positive (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: 15 hr post-infection, the majority of all replicating (i.e. 2K1N + 2K2N) cells were PAD1-positive.
source: Remarkably, 15 hr post-infection, the majority of all replicating (i.e. 2K1N + 2K2N) cells were PAD1-positive (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 5B and supplement.

claim: No indication of a transient cell cycle arrest or intermittent impairment of cell cycle progression was observed in slender cells during differentiation.
source: No indication of a transient cell cycle arrest or intermittent impairment of cell cycle progression was observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claim: After 2 days, more than 90% of dividing trypanosomes were PAD1-positive.
source: After 2 days, more than 90% of dividing trypanosomes were PAD1-positive.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claim: The PAD1 pathway was triggered in replicating slender trypanosomes upon ingestion by the fly, without prior or subsequent cell cycle arrest.
source: Thus, the PAD1 pathway was triggered in replicating slender trypanosomes upon ingestion by the fly, without prior or subsequent cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo differentiation data.

claim: Stumpy trypanosomes remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day after uptake by the tsetse fly, then differentiated to procyclic cells and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days.
source: These cells remained as 1K1N cells in cell cycle arrest for the first day, then differentiated to procyclic cells and re-entered the cell cycle after 2 days.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment comparing stumpy to slender cells.

claim: Four hours after uptake by the tsetse fly, stumpy trypanosomes started expressing EP1:YFP.
source: Four hours after uptake by the tsetse fly, stumpy trypanosomes started expressing EP1:YFP (Figure 6, red).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The fluorescent reporter was visible on 16.2% of stumpy cells after 10 hr, showing that EP expression was initiated before release of cell cycle arrest.
source: The fluorescent reporter was visible on 16.2% of stumpy cells after 10 hr, showing that EP expression was initiated before release of cell cycle arrest (Figure 5C, red; Figure 6, red).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figures 5C and 6.

claim: Uncoupling of EP surface expression from the commitment to differentiation has been reported before.
source: Uncoupling of EP surface expression from the commitment to differentiation has been reported before (Engstler and Boshart, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, only becoming widespread after 24 hr.
source: EP1:YFP expression in slender parasites lagged 12 hr behind stumpy cells, only becoming widespread after 24 hr (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The onset of EP1 expression was shifted, but the kinetics of differentiation were comparable in slender and stumpy parasites.
source: Thus, the onset of EP1 expression was shifted, but the kinetics of differentiation were comparable in slender and stumpy parasites
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo differentiation data.

claim: Activation of the PAD1 pathway preceded developmental progression in slender cells.
source: and activation of the PAD1 pathway also preceded developmental progression in slender cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claim: Expression of PAD1 is essential for differentiation to the procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not.
source: This strongly suggests that expression of PAD1 is essential for differentiation to the procyclic stage, while cell cycle arrest is not.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that slender cells can differentiate without cell cycle arrest.

claim: EP1 expression did not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology.
source: Of note, EP1 expression did not directly correlate with acquisition of procyclic morphology.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment.

claim: At 24 hr, 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive, but EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology.
source: At 24 hr, 9.8% of slender cells were EP1-positive (Figure 6), but the EP1-negative cells frequently exhibited procyclic morphology (Figure 4, upper panels).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vivo differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: GPEET is another procyclic surface protein that is expressed early in the transition from bloodstream stage to procyclic stage cells in the tsetse midgut, before being replaced by EP.
source: GPEET is another procyclic surface protein that is expressed early in the transition from bloodstream stage to procyclic stage cells in the tsetse midgut, before being replaced by EP (Vassella et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A seamless developmental stage transition from the slender bloodstream stage to the procyclic insect stage took place, accompanied by re-organisation of the cytoskeleton and the concomitant switch of swimming styles.
source: This strongly suggests that a seamless developmental stage transition from the slender bloodstream stage to the procyclic insect stage took place, which was accompanied by the typical re-organisation of the cytoskeleton and the concomitant switch of swimming styles (Rotureau et al., 2011; Heddergott et al., 2012; Schuster et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations, supported by citations to previous work on morphological changes.

claim: In the laboratory, differentiation to the procyclic insect stage is routinely induced by the addition of cis-aconitate, removal of glucose, and a temperature drop from 37°C to 27°C.
source: In the laboratory, differentiation to the procyclic insect stage is routinely induced by the addition of cis-aconitate, removal of glucose, and a temperature drop from 37°C to 27°C (Brun et al., 1981; Czichos et al., 1986; Engstler and Boshart, 2004; Qiu et al., 2018; Ziegelbauer et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about laboratory methods, supported by citations.

claim: Slender trypanosomes activated the PAD1 pathway rapidly after receiving the differentiation trigger in vitro, with 9.8% of all parasites being PAD1-positive within 2 hr, and 83.2% after 10 hr.
source: Slender trypanosomes activated the PAD1 pathway rapidly after receiving the trigger, with 9.8% of all parasites being PAD1-positive within 2 hr, and 83.2% after 10 hr.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment.

claim: PAD1 expression peaked after one day (98.3%) in slender cells during in vitro differentiation, and declined thereafter.
source: PAD1 expression peaked after one day (98.3%), and declined thereafter (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 7A and supplement.

claim: Shortly after PAD1 reporter expression, EP1 appeared on the cell surface of 19.6% of all parasites within 8 hr during in vitro differentiation, increasing to 98.3% after 3 days.
source: Shortly after PAD1 reporter expression, EP1 appeared on the cell surface of 19.6% of all parasites within 8 hr, increasing to 98.3% after 3 days (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: PAD1-positive slender parasites did not arrest in the cell cycle during in vitro differentiation, and continued dividing throughout.
source: Throughout the timecourse, PAD1-positive 2K1N and 2K2N cells were continually observed, demonstrating that the PAD1-positive slender parasites did not arrest in the cell cycle, and continued dividing throughout in vitro differentiation to the procyclic stage (Figure 7B, blue).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 7B.

claim: After 3 days of differentiation treatment in vitro, slender trypanosomes had established a proliferating procyclic parasite population.
source: After 3 days of differentiation treatment in vitro, slender trypanosomes had established a proliferating procyclic parasite population, which was further confirmed using morphological analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by morphological data in Figure 7 supplement 3.

claim: Stumpy parasites responded to in vitro cis-aconitate treatment with rapid expression of the EP1:YFP marker, with 28.6% of all cells being positive within 2 hr.
source: By comparison, stumpy parasites (Figure 7A, red) responded to in vitro cis-aconitate treatment with rapid expression of the EP1:YFP marker, with 28.6% of all cells being positive within 2 hr (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: After 1 day of in vitro differentiation, EP1 was present on almost all (96.7%) stumpy trypanosomes.
source: After 1 day, EP1 was present on almost all (96.7%) stumpy trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment.

claim: Stumpy parasites were not dividing during the first day of in vitro differentiation.
source: The cell cycle analysis revealed that these parasites were not dividing, however (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment, supported by data in Figure 7C.

claim: The first stumpy cells re-entered the cell cycle only after 15 hr during in vitro differentiation, and a normal procyclic cell cycle profile was not reached until day 3.
source: The first cells re-entered the cell cycle only after 15 hr, and a normal procyclic cell cycle profile was not reached until day 3.
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro differentiation experiment.

claim: The in vitro differentiation supported the in vivo observations, demonstrating that pleomorphic slender trypanosomes are able to directly differentiate to the procyclic stage without becoming cell cycle-arrested stumpy cells.
source: Thus, the in vitro differentiation supported the in vivo observations, demonstrating that pleomorphic slender trypanosomes are able to directly differentiate to the procyclic stage without becoming cell cycle-arrested stumpy cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro differentiation data, supporting the in vivo findings.

claim: In slender bloodstream parasites, ectopically expressed EP1 does not enter the cell surface, but is retained in endosomes and the flagellar pocket.
source: it has been shown that in slender bloodstream parasites, ectopically expressed EP1 does not enter the cell surface, but is retained in endosomes and the flagellar pocket (Engstler and Boshart, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Lifting of the cell surface access block for EP1 in the slender trypanosome correlates with activation of the PAD1 pathway.
source: Hence, as in stumpy trypanosomes, lifting of the cell surface access block for EP1 in the slender trypanosome correlates with activation of the PAD1 pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that EP1 appears on the surface only after PAD1 activation.

claim: The overall developmental capacity of slender and stumpy cells is comparable both in vitro and in vivo.
source: To summarise, the overall developmental capacity of the two life cycle stages - slender and stumpy cells - is comparable both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo differentiation data.

claim: One trypanosome suffices to produce robust infections of the tsetse vector.
source: We have shown that one trypanosome suffices to produce robust infections of the tsetse vector
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claim: The stumpy stage is not essential for tsetse transmission.
source: and that the stumpy stage is not essential for tsetse transmission.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data showing slender cells can complete the life cycle.

claim: Slender parasites can complete the complex life cycle in the fly with comparable overall success rates and kinetics as the stumpy stage.
source: Slender parasites can complete the complex life cycle in the fly with comparable overall success rates and kinetics as the stumpy stage.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data on transmission indices and differentiation kinetics.

claim: The stumpy stage appears more able to establish initial infections in the fly midgut.
source: Interestingly, the stumpy stage appears more able to establish initial infections in the fly midgut (Figure 2A, column 5, MG)
evidence: This is a finding from the tsetse infection experiments, supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Slender-derived parasites appear to produce salivary gland infections slightly more efficiently (higher TI) than stumpy-derived counterparts.
source: while slender-derived parasites appear to produce salivary gland infections slightly more efficiently (higher amount of salivary gland infections compared to midgut infections, TI) than stumpy-derived counterparts (Figure 2A, column 8, TI).
evidence: This is a finding from the tsetse infection experiments, supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Slender trypanosomes exhibit significantly higher motility compared to stumpy trypanosomes.
source: Slender trypanosomes exhibit significantly higher motility compared to stumpy trypanosomes (Bargul et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Glucose levels are a developmental trigger in addition to cold shock and cis-aconitate.
source: The recent demonstration that glucose levels are a developmental trigger in addition to the well-characterised ones of cold shock and cis-aconitate adds another layer of complexity to the early events during tsetse infection (Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is recent knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stumpy trypanosomes may have evolved as a stress response, with procyclic pathways already activated to increase chances of survival in the fly.
source: It is also of note that a recent review has suggested that stumpy trypanosomes may have evolved as a stress response, with procyclic pathways already activated in order to increase chances of survival in the fly (Quintana et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a recent hypothesis from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The dogma that cell cycle-arrested stumpy cells are the only trypanosomes that infect the tsetse fly has never been experimentally challenged.
source: The dogma that cell cycle-arrested stumpy cells are the only trypanosomes that infect the tsetse fly has never been experimentally challenged
evidence: This is a statement about the history of the field.

claim: There are quite a number of reports that point against an exclusive role for stumpy parasites in the life cycle.
source: although there are quite a number of reports that point against an exclusive role for stumpy parasites in the life cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, which is then supported by specific examples.

claim: Koch's report states that the trypanosome numbers in the blood of human sleeping sickness infections was always very low.
source: Koch's detailed report on the activities of the German sleeping sickness commission sent to East Africa in 1906/7 states that the trypanosome numbers in the blood of human sleeping sickness infections was always very low (Koch, 1909).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: From Koch's data, an average blood parasitaemia between 10 and 100 trypanosome cells/ml can be calculated.
source: From his data, we have calculated an average blood parasitaemia between 10 and 100 trypanosomes cells/ml (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on historical data from Koch's report.

claim: Two or fewer trypanosomes would be present in an average tsetse bloodmeal based on Koch's parasitemia data.
source: This means that two or fewer trypanosomes would be present in an average tsetse bloodmeal, again highlighting the rarity of a tsetse taking up a stumpy cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the calculation of parasitemia and knowledge of bloodmeal volume.

claim: In 1930, Duke discussed the evidence for the essential status of the stumpy stage for tsetse transmission, and his data did not support it.
source: In 1930, Duke discussed the evidence for the essential status of the stumpy stage for tsetse transmission, and his data did not support it (Duke, 1930).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Baker and Robertson in 1957 concluded that neither the morphology nor the intensity of the parasitaemia in the infecting mammal was obviously related to the subsequent infection rates in the tsetse-flies.
source: Further, Baker and Robertson in 1957 compared the infection capability of T. rhodesiense and T. brucei using guinea pig feeding (Baker and Robertson, 1957). They concluded: 'Neither the morphology nor the intensity of the parasitaemia in the infecting mammal was obviously related to the subsequent infection rates in the tsetse-flies'.
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In 1990, Bass and Wang suggested that the stumpy stage may be dispensable for development to the insect stage.
source: In 1990, Bass and Wang suggested that in fact the stumpy stage may be dispensable for development to the insect stage (Bass and Wang, 1991).
evidence: This is historical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The experiments by Bass and Wang were in part inconclusive, mainly because a molecular marker for the stumpy stage was missing.
source: The experiments, however, were in part inconclusive, mainly because a molecular marker for the stumpy stage was missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous work.

claim: The transmission paradox refers to the persistence and circulation of trypanosomiasis in a population even when parasitaemia levels in individuals are low or close to elimination.
source: The above publications all relate to what is nowadays referred to as the transmission paradox, the persistence and circulation of trypanosomiasis in a population even when parasitaemia levels in individuals are low or close to elimination (Capewell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition of a concept in the field, supported by citation.

claim: When parasitaemia is low, stumpy trypanosomes are characteristically absent.
source: When parasitaemia is low, stumpy trypanosomes are characteristically absent
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claim: Solutions to the transmission paradox have been hypothesised to include flawed diagnostic testing, asymptomatic cases, and animal reservoirs.
source: Solutions to the paradox have long been hypothesised and variously include flawed diagnostic testing, asymptomatic cases, and animal reservoirs (Alvar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is knowledge about hypotheses in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Recent work using theoretical modelling suggests that for T. gambiense, trypanosomes residing in the skin of humans could solve the transmission paradox.
source: Recent work using theoretical modelling suggests that for T. gambiense, trypanosomes residing in the skin of humans could solve the problem (Capewell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is recent knowledge from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: There are currently no data available on the number of trypanosomes located in asymptomatic human skin.
source: However, there are currently no data available on the number of trypanosomes located in asymptomatic human skin
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The kinetics of fly uptake of skin-localised trypanosomes have not been explored.
source: nor have the kinetics of fly uptake of skin-localised trypanosomes been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Different tsetse-transmitted trypanosome species reveal rather distinct distributions in the host, such as Trypanosoma congolense preferentially residing in small blood vessels.
source: Also, different tsetse-transmitted trypanosome species reveal rather distinct distributions in the host, such as Trypanosoma congolense preferentially residing in small blood vessels (Banks, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: As tsetse are blood pool feeders, it does not matter if the trypanosomes reside in the skin, fat tissue, or blood.
source: As tsetse are blood pool feeders, it actually does not matter if the trypanosomes reside in the skin, fat tissue, or blood.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of tsetse feeding behavior.

claim: Stumpy cells are not replicative, and their lifetime is limited to roughly 3 days.
source: Furthermore, stumpy cells will inevitably run into an age-related problem. They are not replicative, and their lifetime is limited to roughly 3 days (Turner et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Re-entry into the cell cycle for stumpy cells in the fly is not immediate, but takes at least one day.
source: In the fly, re-entry into the cell cycle is by no means immediate, but takes at least one day.
evidence: This is a finding from the differentiation experiments in this study.

claim: Following induction of cell cycle arrest, the stumpy cells would need to be taken up by the fly within 1 day to be successful.
source: Following induction of cell cycle arrest, the stumpy cells would need to be taken up by the fly within 1 day.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limited lifespan of stumpy cells and the time required for cell cycle re-entry.

claim: Only a subset of rather young stumpy cells would prove successful in the midgut.
source: Thus, only a subset of rather young stumpy cells would prove successful in the midgut.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age-related limitations of stumpy cells.

claim: Only freshly differentiated stumpy cells were used for tsetse infection in the experiments.
source: It is important to note that this is not the case in our experiments, as only freshly differentiated stumpy cells were used for tsetse infection.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: The experiments overestimate the success rate of stumpy stage trypanosomes.
source: Thus, our experiments in fact overestimate the success rate of stumpy stage trypanosomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of using only fresh stumpy cells.

claim: The data provide a possible solution to the transmission paradox without challenging any of the extensive published work on stumpy trypanosomes.
source: It should be stressed that our data provide a possible solution to the transmission paradox without challenging any of the extensive published work on stumpy trypanosomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Slender and stumpy trypanosomes are equally competent for fly passage.
source: We have shown that slender and stumpy trypanosomes are equally competent for fly passage.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data.

claim: The PAD1 pathway has an essential role in preparing both bloodstream stages for differentiation to the procyclic cell stage.
source: The PAD1 pathway has an essential role in preparing both bloodstream stages for differentiation to the procyclic cell stage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differentiation experiments showing PAD1 activation precedes differentiation in both cell types.

claim: For successful passage through the tsetse fly, the stumpy stage is not uniquely required.
source: For successful passage through the tsetse fly, however, the stumpy stage is not uniquely required.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data showing slender cells can complete the life cycle.

claim: Trypanosoma congolense infects tsetse flies without manifesting a cell cycle-arrested stumpy stage.
source: Along similar lines, it is worth noting that Trypanosoma congolense, the principal causative agent of the cattle plague nagana, infects tsetse flies without manifesting a cell cycle-arrested stumpy stage (Rotureau and Van Den Abbeele, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The essential biological function of the stumpy life cycle stage in T. brucei may be quorum sensing (SIF)-dependent control of population size in the host, not transmission.
source: Thus, the essential biological function of the stumpy life cycle stage in T. brucei may not be transmission, but rather quorum sensing (SIF)-dependent control of population size in the host.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biological function of the stumpy stage based on the findings.

claim: The capacity for inducing cell cycle arrest at the single cell level might have been important for the evolution of antigenic variation.
source: The capacity for inducing cell cycle arrest at the single cell level might actually have been important for the evolution of antigenic variation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary implications.

claim: Not all trypanosome species develop a stumpy life cycle stage.
source: As not all trypanosome species develop a stumpy life cycle stage (Rotureau and Van Den Abbeele, 2013)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Density-dependent differentiation at the population level may be a later innovation in evolution, specific to the T. brucei group.
source: density-dependent differentiation at the population level may well be a later innovation in evolution, and specific to the T. brucei group.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary history.

claim: The work evidences a high degree of plasticity in the life cycle of an important parasite.
source: In conclusion, our work evidences a high degree of plasticity in the life cycle of an important parasite.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The trypanosome life cycle is not rigid.
source: It shows that the trypanosome life cycle is not rigid
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A revised and more flexible view of the trypanosome life cycle may help solve a longstanding puzzle in parasitology.
source: and we have proposed a revised and more flexible view of the trypanosome life cycle that may help solve a longstanding puzzle in parasitology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the implications of the findings for the field.
